Okay, while I said I liked this game, [b]I think in terms of recommendation, this is more a "maybe" than an outright "yes."[/b] There are several things to consider before you purchase this one, and while I ultimately think you'll enjoy the experience either way, you may be slightly frustrated by at least one or two of these points. I know I was. 

(-) First, the game is short. It took me less than 4 hours to finish it, and that's with several long cut scenes. Speaking of those cut scenes... pay attention to them. I didn't, because some of them seemed pointless, and that led me to the only time I felt truly stuck in this game LOL.

(+) You play as an operator in the FDI, and the entire gameplay involves sitting in front of your computer, connecting dots, and solving puzzles. I absolutely loved it. It was fresh and interesting, and the feeling of things connecting and unraveling was really fun. I actually wish we had more of it—I would've gladly played more hours of more cases, slowly connecting them to this huge conspiracy. It made me hope that someone would make an entire mystery murder game (as opposed to a conspiracy) as "the guy in the chair," slowly unraveling everything and helping the "heroes" solve the mystery. 

(-/+) For a game that's sitting in front of your computer... the stakes are high and so is the tension. I actually got really anxious at parts, in a way that doesn't really happen with most games because, the way everything is set up, WE are Tenner. So I felt like there was a gun aimed at [i]me[/i] at times, LOL. For me, this was a point in favor of the game, but if you're looking for a more relaxed experience, this may not be it. 

(-/+) The ending. Personally? Not a fan. Oh, I loved the reveal. The minute [i]I[/i] started connecting the dots, my stomach dropped. 10/10 for that. But everything after that?... I will be playing the next game, if there is one, but overall, [spoiler]I am not really the kind of person to enjoy an "everybody died" ending. After all the brilliant puzzle solving, I wanted these characters to have a good ending. I have seen people talk about how this was actually a good ending - how Hal is still thwarting the organization 30 years later, and that's realistic and optimistic but damn. I got attached to [i]these[/i] characters. I wanted to see them happy, even if we fail to totally crush the bad guys in the end of the game. And I wanted to understand what the goal of the "bad guys" in this game is, and I don't. They're evil people, but... why are they doing what they're doing? No clue. Which is another thing I don't like. For me, a game needs to be able to stand on its own, even if it's part of a larger narrative. [/spoiler] Essentially, this felt like a game meant to [i]set up[/i] another game, and truthfully, I don't like that.

review_text_raw:
Hello developers,

I just finished playing your game on the Switch, and I immediately bought the Steam version to add to my library. The game's atmosphere and narrative pacing really drew me in, and the background music was perfectly fitting. Because of this, I'm happy to leave a positive review, though it also left me with higher expectations.

 [spoiler]
The game is about four hours long, and playing it felt more like watching a movie. However, as a game, it offered too few choices for the player. During my play through, I tried to deliberately not answer the supervisor's calls or even pretended to be a 'good kid' to see if there was a way to betray HAL. But the game didn't give me any more options. I believe that in an interactive story game, player choices and their consequences are its true charm and what keeps players engaged.
The bomb disposal segment really stood out. I felt a strong sense of immersion and genuinely enjoyed being able to help someone. It's a shame that, probably due to the game's length, such a brilliant sequence only happened once.
The core puzzle was very cleverly designed, and its reveal was absolutely an adrenaline rush. I completely understand what you, as developers, wanted players to feel with that ending—the horror, the profound sense of melancholy, the sadness for the characters, and the lingering regret that a bigger enemy wasn't truly dealt with. However, even after experiencing all that, I still wished players could help the characters achieve a good ending. I truly love these characters.
Overall, this is a fantastic game! I really hope to play more from you in the future!
[/spoiler]

A Thriller That Rekindled My Creative Spark

🖥️ 🔍 ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆
🕹️ Great on Steam Deck

One of the reasons I became a software developer was the dream of eventually making games. Over the years, there have only been a handful of titles that truly reignited that spark and made game development feel possible again. The Operator unexpectedly became one of those games.

From its presentation to its atmosphere, the game pulled me in quickly, but it was the storytelling, especially toward the final stretch, that really hit. The ending was a genuine chef’s kiss. Not because it wrapped everything neatly, but because it didn’t. When it was over, I felt that familiar disappointment that only comes from wanting more. More answers about HAL. More about The Ghost. More about the Organization and where this world could go next.

I understand why some players felt like they were simply going through the motions to push the story forward. For me, curiosity carried the experience. I wanted to poke at every decision, even knowing the branching paths were not especially deep or wide. The choices still felt meaningful enough to keep me engaged and questioning the outcome.

If you’re looking for a short, focused thriller with an intriguing premise, believable characters, and a strong audiovisual presentation, The Operator is absolutely worth your time. Especially on sale. It’s the kind of game that lingers in your head after the credits roll, and quietly nudges your creative mind into motion.

review_text_raw:
*Well made thriller, intriguing story, albeit flawed and very short*

The Operator has you play as Evan Tanner, the titular operator of the fictional FDI. Your task is to sit behind a computer and conduct forensic inestigations with state-of-the-art tools to help your colleagues in the field. 
You quickly become part of a major conspiracy and need to uncover the secrets of a series of missing cases and murders.

I did enjoy my time with the games but it has a fair amount of shortcomings, my main issues being the short length and abrupt ending.

The game mainly involves you getting sent files such as video feeds by FDI agents that you need to sleuth through to uncover important information such as the ID of a suspect. The tasks are pretty varied to keep it from getting stale. However, the game does not flesh out the gameplay. Many tasks are done only once, making it feel fairly shallow. 

The main focus is clearly the story. It is intriguing and does enough to keep you hooked. 
The voice actors do a good job portraying their characters, although they can feel underdeveloped. While I did enjoy it for the most part, it felt rushed to me. The already fast pacing picks up at the end, and then the game just ends, leaving many unanswered questions. The game also teases multiple endings by giving you the illusion of choices throughout the story, but there is only a singular storyline.

The presentation is well done and immersive thanks to the visuals and sound design. The soundtrack also does a good job accompanying the story by kicking in at important beats.

As I mentioned a few times, the game is overly short; you could probably beat it in three hours. For the story it's setting up, I feel like it'd need more time to tell it in full.

Overall, the Operator gets a slight recommend from me. But maybe wait for a discount for this one.

review_text_raw:
It's worth playing as it isn't very long. The gameplay concept and execution are really good. The voice acting is pretty decent and makes the visual novel style content engaging to consume in addition to the gameplay mechanics. They have some pretty good tricks to flesh out the experience and make it feel more "real" while still managing to keeping the game very lo-fi...

I think it had a lot more potential than it tapped into. A very common criticism will be linearity and lack of player choice or replayability. There are a few moments where you can alter the outcome of an event that feels like it should have a more meaningful impact on the story, but the impact on the overall narrative is actually very little.  I also feel they were very close to allowing you to play the detective by doing your own extracurricular investigating, but then they sort of throw that out by having a character just be like "I bet you didn't notice THIS!" It's like... actually I did notice it and I wanted to have my moment of feeling like a genius. I think this is something that the Ace Attorney games do a little better.... while still railroading you into a very specific solution and solution path, they at least make you feel like you figured things out and make it feel rewarding. I think this game could have done at least more of that if not going as far as to actually add in more optional discovery and unprompted use of the information you gathered.

I'll also say that while this is a pretty good standalone narrative game concept, it feels like something I'd like to see integrated into a bigger game that doesn't play exclusively like this.

review_text_raw:
This game is top notch. As an old school adventure fan this felt like a true Rise of the Dragon, Jeff Tunnell style game which has been sorely lacking in the current market. What I mean by that specifically is that the post-Life is Strange adventure genre has had a long period of hammy, melodramatic social messaging meant to impress small cliques of games journalists for accolades in their astroturfed outlets. The REAL culprit was ABUSE! Or HOMOPHOBIA! Or RACISM! And the game was a METAPHOR! This plot device was not terribly interesting to begin with but due to the applause and funding that comes to such projects, it left us with a decade of such tripe as developers scratched and clawed to be next in line at the Attaboy Club, with each new offering being more hamfisted and alarmist than the last (check my review of 'Jessika' for a hilarious instance of this).

The Operator, however, is just a good old fashioned hard boiled story about cover ups and corruption.  It has a couple of flaws, the primary one being the blurred out bokeh filters meant to act as cutscenes. There is a sorta-kinda in-story explanation for this, and a reason for it to justify a later puzzle, but really it just comes across as a way to avoid paying for cutscenes and as a way to bridge days together, which is understandable enough for a small team with not a lot of money. In future, I'd recommend bridging the days with some kind of interactive option at the character's apartment or neighborhood, or by just using comic book style art for the cutscenes. In any case that complaint is a nothing burger, the game is well worth it and I look forward to more!

review_text_raw:
The Operator, developed by Bureau 81 and published by Bureau 81 together with indienova, is a tightly focused narrative puzzle game that transforms the quiet, procedural work of intelligence analysis into a tense and engaging thriller. Rather than placing players in the role of an action hero or field agent, the game casts them as a desk-bound operator, someone whose power comes not from physical presence but from information, observation, and deduction. This shift in perspective defines the entire experience, creating a game that feels intimate, cerebral, and deliberately restrained.

You play as Evan Tanner, a newly recruited operator working for the fictional Federal Department of Intelligence. Your job is to support agents in the field by analysing data, processing evidence, and drawing connections that others might miss. The game unfolds almost entirely through Evan’s workstation, presented as a simulated computer desktop filled with databases, analysis tools, messaging systems, and case files. This interface-driven approach immediately sets the tone: instead of cinematic spectacle, The Operator relies on immersion through routine, making the player feel like they are genuinely sitting at a government terminal late at night, piecing together fragments of truth.

Gameplay revolves around solving a series of cases that gradually escalate in complexity and importance. Early tasks feel procedural—identifying suspects, tracing movements, or cross-referencing records—but as the story unfolds, patterns begin to emerge and the stakes rise. Players are required to closely read documents, examine photos and videos, search databases, and interpret subtle clues hidden in plain sight. The puzzles reward attentiveness and logical reasoning, often asking players to synthesize information from multiple sources rather than relying on a single obvious answer. When a breakthrough occurs, it feels earned, the result of careful thought rather than trial and error.

As the narrative progresses, the game shifts from isolated casework into a broader conspiracy. A mysterious hacker begins to interfere with FDI systems, raising questions about surveillance, authority, and the reliability of the information you’re working with. This transition adds narrative tension without abandoning the game’s grounded tone. The story remains largely linear, but it is effectively paced, allowing suspense to build gradually as seemingly unrelated assignments reveal deeper connections. Dialogue and character interactions are understated, delivered through calls, messages, and system prompts rather than dramatic cutscenes, which reinforces the feeling that you are always working behind the scenes.

One of the game’s greatest strengths is how convincingly it uses its interface as both a storytelling and gameplay tool. Every window, search bar, and analysis program feels purposeful, and learning how to use these tools becomes part of the experience. While some mechanics are simplified or exaggerated for gameplay purposes, they remain believable within the fiction, maintaining immersion. The design encourages players to slow down, double-check assumptions, and think critically—mistakes often stem from overlooking details rather than misunderstanding mechanics.

Visually, The Operator embraces a minimalist, utilitarian aesthetic inspired by older operating systems and institutional software. The interface is dense but readable, intentionally lacking visual flair in favor of authenticity. This design choice may feel dry to some players, but it suits the game’s themes perfectly, emphasizing bureaucracy, control, and the monotony of surveillance work. Subtle audio cues, ambient hums, and restrained music enhance tension without distracting from concentration, allowing the player’s focus to remain on the task at hand.

In terms of pacing, the game strikes a careful balance. It is compact, typically completed in a handful of hours, but it avoids feeling rushed. Each case builds naturally on the last, and the increasing narrative weight keeps momentum strong. The linear structure limits replayability, as choices rarely branch into significantly different outcomes, but this also allows the developers to maintain tight narrative control and deliver a coherent, focused story without filler.

Community reception reflects appreciation for the game’s originality and execution. Players who enjoy detective work, mystery narratives, and “games on a computer” style experiences frequently praise its atmosphere and puzzle design. Criticism tends to focus on its short length, limited player agency, and occasional moments where immersion is broken by game-like constraints. Even so, these issues rarely overshadow the strengths of the experience, particularly for players aligned with its intended audience.

Taken as a whole, The Operator is a confident and distinctive narrative puzzle game that finds tension in observation rather than action. It succeeds by committing fully to its premise, turning data analysis and desk work into compelling gameplay through thoughtful design and strong thematic focus. While it may not appeal to players seeking open-ended systems or high replay value, it offers a memorable, tightly constructed experience for those who enjoy slow-burn storytelling, logical deduction, and the quiet unease of uncovering truths from behind a screen.

Rating: 9/10

Fantastic game, very enjoyable. You play as a call-operator for the "FDI", helping field agents to analyse the evidence they're obtaining. It's like you're at a screen with a headset, using the information to help solve crimes, and eventually, to get to the heart of the growing conspiracy that you begin to suspect within the FDI itself...

review_text_raw:
*spoiler free*

A very enjoyable detective thriller that's spent mostly looking at the same computer screen, tastefully emulating a simple, proprietary FBI desktop you'd see in the background of 90s movies. Even so, the gameplay is varied, as you gain access to more and more tools and programs to use in your cases, and the tasks or cases themselves vary a lot. 
One particular case that involves a manual was one of the most memorable gaming experiences I've had recently. It was very tense and had me fully immersed in my current task. You'll know it when you get to it.

Speaking of immersion, you occasionally get breaks from the screen (as you should in real life as well) as your character steps away to end the day and get home, or walk to a nearby destination. These intermissions are very well done and put you in the character's shoes, not to mention let the both of you unwind before the next day of cracking cases.

The mystery is engaging and gives you just enough clues at just the right pace to let you put the puzzle pieces together yourself. Don't take this as a negative, this is the game rewarding you for paying attention, using your notepad and attempting to connect the dots yourself.

For the price of one movie ticket and a box of popcorn you'll get much more than the average flick and support a great developer. I hope to see more in the future.

Editing because I forgot to mention:
The soundtrack and audio work is FANTASTIC, listening to it now.

review_text_raw:
[h1][b] TLDR: Sells itself as an investigative puzzler but delivers a mostly on-rails visual novel experience. The handful of genuine puzzles are great, making their scarcity all the more frustrating.
[/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Neat investigative puzzles (ENHANCE….ENHANCE)
➕Some nice puzzles, like bomb defuse

[h1]NEUTRALS: [/h1]
🔹Story is good, but a bit too on-rails and hand-holding

[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Lots of unskippable intentionally blurry cutscenes leaves a cheap or vague feeling
➖Some reveals are not as big as they should be simply because you wouldn’t know things that your character would know

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world takes place entirely from a computer screen and is set in the 90s, we’re talking older CRT monitor screens. There’s not much exploration to be found, as you work for the government and everything is pretty locked down. I’d say the world is a bit basic and simple, only serving as a UI to show some puzzles. 

The narrative has some good parts. You play as Evan Tanner, a Federal Department of Investigation (FDI) operator, in which your job is to assist field agents. You very quickly learn that there’s something going on and you are enlisted, whether you want to or not, to uncover the truth. 
So while I did enjoy the story to an extent, any scene not at the computer and is told through a characters eyes is a blurry mess of objects that are nearly undecipherable. This could be something related to the story, but I don’t want to give the game the benefit of the doubt here and say that it worsens the experience. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The gameplay seems pretty cool at first, but you quickly realize how on-rails the game is. Essentially, this is a glorified visual novel with a few puzzles sprinkled in. At first, I felt like Garcia from Criminal Minds - I was the internet sleuth assisting agents in the field by giving them on-the-fly information to help with cases. But unfortunately, the game isn’t as cool as that. 
The loop consists of you having a conversation, being presented with evidence, and then using the 2-3 tools at your disposal to answer a question presented by the conversation. For example, you’ll need to identify a killer and a victim by scanning their faces to get their names, then look them up in the FDI database. Same thing with licenses plates or analyzing footage/pictures. It does sound very cool, but I can’t emphasize enough the on-rails experience and lack of deep puzzle mechanics. This is more of a game focused on the narrative. 

The difficulty is forgiving. I’m pretty sure I made every wrong choice in the game, yet still made it to the end. I literally messed up a [spoiler]bomb defuse and got an agent killed[/spoiler]. Whoops. Despite these consequences, this doesn’t seem like it impacted the game as much and wasn’t mentioned again other than a few brief times after the fact. 

[h1] [b] Graphics (Quality/Technical) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Being that the game is from the point of view of a computer screen and all “Real” scenes are a blurry mess, I’d say the quality isn’t great. What footage you do see is grainy 90’s-era quality, but aside from that the computer UI is good and crisp. 

On the technical side, I had no issues, encountered no bugs, and ran the game without issues. 

1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD  

[h1] [b] Audio – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The music isn’t really noticeable, but it does increase in intensity during high-drama parts. 

There is a lot of voice acting, and it all sounds good. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [2/10] [/b] [/h1]
Not a lot of replay value here, unless you want to redo the puzzles again for achievements. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The Operator is described as a game with detective/investigation, and puzzle elements. I’d estimate the game to be about 70% story/narrative focus, 20% puzzles, and 10% deducing or investigating. I’d say that Operator is an okay game, but I was a bit disappointed by the mystery and investigative sides. This is very much a visual novel game more than anything, and as someone that likes visual novels, I was expecting more to use my brain to make deductions instead of clicking pre-defined replies. 

The game does have a few puzzles. I’d say maybe ~10 at the most, and despite that small number, I found them to be good puzzles. Analyzing gunpowder was really cool. Defusing a bomb on the fly was also great. If the game was more focused on gameplay like that, then I’d give it a much higher score, but these are the highest highs that The Operator offers, and there’s only a few of them. 

The real focus of the game is on the narrative. While I wouldn’t consider the narrative to be bad, there were a few parts that were either ridiculously obvious, or a missed opportunity. 
Obvious, because of metagaming - anyone who watches mystery shows knows that there’s only so many characters who could be the culprit due to you the show introducing them to the viewer. Same concept here, it’s obviously going to be the handful of people you know about already. 
Missed opportunity because you as the player only know what you know. One part in particular [spoiler]has the player finding out his apartment is being watched with a camera, and you have to identify whose apartment it is[/spoiler]. Well how can you possibly figure that out without knowing anything about the characters' life, nor ever having been there? Dumb. 

Overall, I do recommend The Operator, but it’s important that you know what you’re going into. This is NOT about deduction or investigating, and that’s not necessarily a bad thing, but I feel the game presents itself in a way that it’s something that it isn’t. 

[h1] [b] Recommend? (Price) [Y/N] [/b] [/h1]
[h1]Yes[/h1]
$14 base price is a bit much for a ~5 hour game with very low replay value. Wait for a sale. Around ~$5-7 would be a good point.

The narrative has some good parts. You play as Evan Tanner, a Federal Department of Investigation (FDI) operator, in which your job is to assist field agents. You very quickly learn that there’s something going on and you are enlisted, whether you want to or not, to uncover the truth. So while I did enjoy the story to an extent, any scene not at the computer and is told through a characters eyes is a blurry mess of objects that are nearly undecipherable. This could be something related to the story, but I don’t want to give the game the benefit of the doubt here and say that it worsens the experience. [h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1] The gameplay seems pretty cool at first, but you quickly realize how on-rails the game is. Essentially, this is a glorified visual novel with a few puzzles sprinkled in. At first, I felt like Garcia from Criminal Minds - I was the internet sleuth assisting agents in the field by giving them on-the-fly information to help with cases. But unfortunately, the game isn’t as cool as that. The loop consists of you having a conversation, being presented with evidence, and then using the 2-3 tools at your disposal to answer a question presented by the conversation. For example, you’ll need to identify a killer and a victim by scanning their faces to get their names, then look them up in the FDI database. Same thing with licenses plates or analyzing footage/pictures. It does sound very cool, but I can’t emphasize enough the on-rails experience and lack of deep puzzle mechanics. This is more of a game focused on the narrative. The difficulty is forgiving. I’m pretty sure I made every wrong choice in the game, yet still made it to the end. I literally messed up a [spoiler]bomb defuse and got an agent killed[/spoiler]. Whoops. Despite these consequences, this doesn’t seem like it impacted the game as much and wasn’t mentioned again other than a few brief times after the fact. [h1] [b] Graphics (Quality/Technical) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1] Being that the game is from the point of view of a computer screen and all “Real” scenes are a blurry mess, I’d say the quality isn’t great. What footage you do see is grainy 90’s-era quality, but aside from that the computer UI is good and crisp. On the technical side, I had no issues, encountered no bugs, and ran the game without issues. 1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD [h1] [b] Audio – [6/10] [/b] [/h1] The music isn’t really noticeable, but it does increase in intensity during high-drama parts. There is a lot of voice acting, and it all sounds good. [h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [2/10] [/b] [/h1] Not a lot of replay value here, unless you want to redo the puzzles again for achievements. [h1] [b] Final Verdict – [6/10] [/b] [/h1] The Operator is described as a game with detective/investigation, and puzzle elements. I’d estimate the game to be about 70% story/narrative focus, 20% puzzles, and 10% deducing or investigating. I’d say that Operator is an okay game, but I was a bit disappointed by the mystery and investigative sides. This is very much a visual novel game more than anything, and as someone that likes visual novels, I was expecting more to use my brain to make deductions instead of clicking pre-defined replies. The game does have a few puzzles. I’d say maybe ~10 at the most, and despite that small number, I found them to be good puzzles. Analyzing gunpowder was really cool. Defusing a bomb on the fly was also great. If the game was more focused on gameplay like that, then I’d give it a much higher score, but these are the highest highs that The Operator offers, and there’s only a few of them. The real focus of the game is on the narrative. While I wouldn’t consider the narrative to be bad, there were a few parts that were either ridiculously obvious, or a missed opportunity. Obvious, because of metagaming - anyone who watches mystery shows knows that there’s only so many characters who could be the culprit due to you the show introducing them to the viewer. Same concept here, it’s obviously going to be the handful of people you know about already. Missed opportunity because you as the player only know what you know. One part in particular [spoiler]has the player finding out his apartment is being watched with a camera, and you have to identify whose apartment it is[/spoiler]. Well how can you possibly figure that out without knowing anything about the characters' life, nor ever having been there? Dumb. Overall, I do recommend The Operator, but it’s important that you know what you’re going into. This is NOT about deduction or investigating, and that’s not necessarily a bad thing, but I feel the game presents itself in a way that it’s something that it isn’t. [h1] [b] Recommend? (Price) [Y/N] [/b] [/h1] [h1]Yes[/h1] $14 base price is a bit much for a ~5 hour game with very low replay value. Wait for a sale. Around ~$5-7 would be a good point. Best way I can describe this game is a virtual escape room. There's hints and clues but the nature of the puzzles ensure it's very difficult to brute force the solutions. The puzzles are never too difficult (save for maybe 1 in the halfway point of the game, but that 1 is oh so rewarding when you get it) and are always rewarding, but they never hold the players hand too much, a perfect balance.

My ONLY complaint with the game is that I wish there was more of it; more cases to crack on the side and more digging around I can do into cases that maybe wouldn't effect the story. This game shines when it allows you to use all your tools to crack a case and I wish there was more of that. 

Overall took me 4 hours to beat, but it was a great 4 hours. Would recommend to anyone who enjoys escape rooms, puzzle games, or immersive experiences.
